speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as ChatGPT are expected to affect student coursework and open-book assessments and, if so, how; (b) what challenges and opportunities exist in the educational and skills landscape due to the rise of such AI; and (c) what is being done to inculcate life skills, soft skills, and other competencies so that human workers can remain competitive and relevant amidst a landscape encompassing international competition and AI advancements.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether there are cases of cheating among students in schools and Institutes of Higher Learning in relation to the artificial intelligence chatbot ChatGPT; and (b) what measures are put in place to detect plagiarism.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked the Minister for Education (a) whether the Ministry is studying the trend of the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology among international student bodies to cheat in exams and assignments; (b) whether similar instances have happened locally; (c) how does the Ministry plan to address this issue in Singapore’s education system; and (d) how will the Ministry guide educators to harness the use of AI to enhance learning while ensuring that students do not misuse AI technology for cheating or any other unethical behaviour.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah
text: asked the Minister for Education what are schools doing to prevent potential abuses of artificial intelligence chatbots such as ChatGPT.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also professional discussion groups amongst our educators to explore its use in the education setting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, our educators will still teach students to understand fundamental concepts and guide students against developing an over-reliance on technological tools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, just like how a calculator supports students' capacity for learning mathematics but that does not replace the need for our students to first master basic mathematical operations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ChatGPT can be a useful tool for learning only when students have mastered basic concepts and thinking skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In a more uncertain world, we must also teach our students to embrace and learn to work with tools in the new normal that have a range of outcomes beyond a deterministic outcome like a calculator.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This would extend to AI tools that will increase in pervasiveness and may not provide only deterministic answers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our educators will also help students understand how AI tools like ChatGPT work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As ChatGPT can provide inaccurate or biased output depending on its inputs, students need to be discerning and critically assess its output for accuracy and objectivity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Schools and IHLs adopt a range of practices to guard against misuse of this technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In their daily work, students are taught the importance of integrity and the harmful impact and consequences of plagiarism.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our IHLs have varied modes of assessment including examinations, presentations and projects that require analysis, field notes and observational details that cannot be generated easily by AI technology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our schools equip students with important skills such as assimilating concepts and applying them to new and dynamic situations, self-directed and collaborative learning, inventive thinking, relationship management and cross-cultural skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: All these efforts are sustained as students enter our IHLs, where the curriculum has also been enhanced to help students develop baseline digital competencies, as well as life skills to better navigate work and adulthood.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our schools and IHLs will continue to equip students with digital competencies and values to enable them to harness technology confidently and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And finally, Mr Speaker, Sir, for the record, this answer has been provided by my hardworking MOE officers and not by ChatGPT.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To be honest, when I started writing the Parliamentary Question (PQ), I was concerned with ChatGPT being used pervasively by students and giving them an advantage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But over time, after using it myself extensively and testing it against my essay questions and seeing how it can be caught for plagiarism, I understand that it is quite important that we teach our students the importance of using AI-related tools.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I think that this is the wave that we should embark on.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have discussion groups within the professional community on how to harness the potential of such technologies for us to improve the education system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Similarly, we would also like to equip our students with the skillsets to learn how to use this responsibly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Because as I have mentioned, in the new world, it is not just about trying to find a deterministic answer like learning how to use a calculator, where one plus one always equals to two.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the new world, we need to be able to work with a range of possible outcomes and consider them holistically.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why, I have been emphasising to all my students and teachers that the new skillsets for us in this generation is learning how to discover, to distil and finally, to discern.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And if possible, to develop or create something new in the process because our value-add today is not about trying to answer yesterday's problems with yesterday's answer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our value-add is how to create tomorrow's solutions for tomorrow's challenges ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These are new skillsets that we must all acquire and help our students to acquire.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And do the students know this as well?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In what way has the communication been done?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And finally, have any cases been detected so far and what are the penalties?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Cheating may take the form of conventional cheating or cheating may take new forms, like that enabled by new technologies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, this is always an evergreen challenge that we have to overcome.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it requires two parts in the solutioning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first part is how to detect cheating is our examinations, tests and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And that is, again, a bit like a "cat and mouse" game where if you improve your technologies, the other side may also try to come up with other new and innovation ways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think the more important aspect is how we educate our people to understand the fundamental values, hold on to the fundamental values, how we impart them the values such that they understand why they are doing what they are doing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the learning process, it is not about coming out with an answer to give the answer and submit it to the teachers or to the examination board.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What is more important is also the process of trying to get to the answer and how you derive that answer.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And even then, they must be able to go back to the three "D"s that I mentioned: discover, distil and discern.
